about: Coaching tips written by the Spin Off team for SpinOff_AI (feedback_database.csv, 201 tips) and its k-NN index (feedback_knn.pkl): X holds each tip's range midpoints of [shot type id, speed mph, spin rpm, launch angle deg, quality 0-100], standardized with mean and scale. The app takes the k nearest tips and shows the first one written for the same kick type. skip lists tips about fatigue or a whole session, which one kick cannot show.
tip: Use the laces of your boot and drive through the ball — your contact is too soft. Plant your standing foot directly beside the ball and commit your whole leg into the swing.
Good attempt — increase your leg swing speed. Drive the knee over the ball before striking and let your kicking leg follow through fully toward the target.
Very gentle contact — you may be pulling back at the last moment. Commit fully: once you start the swing, drive all the way through. Trust the technique.
Good effort — increase your follow-through by letting your kicking foot swing up toward your chest after contact. The leg should not stop at the ball.
Decent power for your age. Lock your ankle at contact and drive the knee over the ball for more pace. A rigid ankle transfers energy directly into the ball.
Speed is developing well. Work on a longer run-up to generate more momentum — the power in a shot comes mostly from the approach, not just the leg swing.
Solid power — now work on hitting the same spot every time. Pick a small target and try to replicate this exact strike 10 times in a row.
Strong strike. At this speed, accuracy becomes your next priority. Aim for the corners rather than just hitting hard — placement wins games.
Good pace with low spin — this is a flat, unpredictable drive that keepers hate. Keep replicating this contact and then work on placement to a corner.
Excellent pace — now make every strike count. Pick a specific corner before you shoot and drive the ball exactly there. Power without placement is wasted.
You have the speed but the technique broke down slightly. Check your contact duration and strike offset — the power is there, now make it cleaner.
That is serious pace for your age. Keep building leg strength and your speed will increase month by month. Stay consistent with this technique.
You are scuffing the ball — contact lasted too long. Strike sharply with a locked ankle, like you are stamping a seal, not dragging across the ball.
Slightly dragging through contact. Tighten your ankle and snap your foot through — the contact should feel like a sharp punch, not a sweep.
Long, soft contact means a loss of energy. A quality power shot has a very short, explosive contact. Try making the contact sound sharper — a clean snap.
Off-center contact — you are striking the side of the ball. Aim to hit through the exact center of the ball with the flat of your laces.
Slightly off-center. Slow the approach down and check where your laces meet the ball. The sweet spot is the dead center — visualize it before you strike.
Too flat — you are topping the ball. Lean back slightly and strike just below the center of the ball to get it rising at 15-25 degrees.
Angle is very flat. For a power shot, aim for 15-25 degrees. Tilt your body back a fraction and contact the lower half of the ball.
Too much height — you are striking too far under the ball. Move your contact point up slightly and lean your body forward over the ball.
Way too steep — this ball is going over the bar. Drive through the center of the ball with your body forward. Think horizontal, not vertical.
Too much spin on what should be a flat drive. Your foot is wrapping around the ball at contact — square your ankle and strike straight through.
Unintended sidespin detected. For a power shot, you want minimal spin. Keep your ankle locked and foot facing the target squarely at contact.
Near-perfect power shot. Consistent contact, great angle, real pace. Push the speed higher by generating more hip rotation on your swing.
Textbook power shot — minimal spin, perfect angle, serious pace. This is exactly what you want from a driving strike. Repeat it every session.
Elite-level power shot for your age group. You are striking with pace and keeping it on target. Aim for the bottom corners to make it unstoppable.
Inconsistent technique across your session. Your best kicks are great — focus on making every kick look like your best one. Build a pre-kick routine.
Consistent and controlled. Work on a pre-kick routine — same steps, same body shape every time — to lock in this technique under pressure.
That was a mishit — do not rush. Slow down your run-up, look at the ball all the way through contact, and restart with a controlled strike.
Big miskick — high spin and low speed means your foot caught the side of the ball. Reset, breathe, and strike through the center next time.
You are just starting out — great that you are practicing. Focus on one thing: strike with your laces, not your toe. Everything else will follow.
Good angle and decent pace. The next step is increasing leg swing speed. Try taking a longer run-up for more momentum into the ball.
Workable but pace needs work. Focus on a full leg swing and locked ankle — speed comes from technique, not from trying harder.
Very gentle impact — you may be pulling back at the last moment. Commit fully to the kick. Trust your technique and drive straight through.
Strong consistent power shot. Work on always aiming for a specific target — drive to a corner, not just into goal. Precision wins matches.
Outstanding strike. Minimal spin, pace, and perfect angle. This is what a match-quality power shot looks like. Practice placing it to both corners.
Solid power and angle. Next challenge: repeat this five times in a row hitting the same corner. Consistency under repetition is the key skill.
Power shot needs a reset. Slow everything right down, focus only on where your laces meet the ball, and build back up from controlled contact.
Barely any curve — your foot is not wrapping around the ball. Strike with the inside of your foot and follow through across your body to generate spin.
Minimal curl. To develop more spin, contact the ball with the inside of your foot at its mid-line and sweep your leg across on the follow-through.
Developing curl — you can see the ball bending. Work on generating 350+ rpm by wrapping your foot more aggressively through the contact zone.
Good start on the curve. Push the follow-through further across your body after contact — that is what increases the spin rate consistently.
Curl is coming. Make sure you strike with the inside of your foot — not the toe or the laces — for the most spin transfer onto the ball.
Nice curl developing. At this spin rate you will see real movement in flight. Keep the speed controlled — too much pace kills the curve.
Strong curve technique. The ball is bending well. Now work on consistency — can you hit this spin rate on every single attempt?
Excellent curl — high spin rate with good control. At this level, work on disguising the shot direction so the keeper cannot read which way it bends.
Elite curve ball for your age. This level of spin with controlled speed is what professional free-kick specialists achieve. Keep it up.
Too much pace is killing your curve — the ball cannot bend at this speed. Slow your strike to 35-45 mph and let the spin do the work.
Good spin but slightly too fast for maximum curl. A slower, more wrapped strike will produce more visible bend through the flight.
Your spin axis suggests topspin rather than sidespin. For a curve, strike with the inside of your foot at the ball's mid-line, not underneath it.
Backspin detected on what should be a sidespin curve. Adjust your foot angle — contact should be on the inside of the ball, not the underside.
Angle too flat for a curve — it needs height to show its bend in flight. Strike slightly below the ball's mid-line to launch it at 20-35 degrees.
Too much height on the curve. Get your body more over the ball and contact at the mid-point, not below — otherwise it sails harmlessly over.
Beautiful technique — right spin, right pace, right angle. This ball will bend away from the keeper. Practice it from different field positions.
Well-balanced curve ball — the spin and speed ratio is excellent. Focus on landing this in a 2-foot square target area consistently.
Outstanding curl. Combine this with your power shot in the same session — switching between them makes you completely unpredictable.
Your foot angle is not wrapping around the ball enough. Think about brushing the side of the ball from inside-to-outside with your foot across the contact.
The curl is there but needs more follow-through. After contact, your kicking leg should sweep across your body — do not stop it at the ball.
Consistent curl with good spin. Practice on a stationary ball first, then moving, then under match pressure — build up the difficulty gradually.
Great curve consistency. Try varying the degree of bend to beat different defensive setups — a tight curl close post vs a sweeping far-post bend.
This is a match-quality curve ball. The spin, pace, and angle combination would be very difficult for a keeper to read. Excellent work.
Curve ball contact was lost entirely. Reset — take a slow practice swing and feel where the inside of your foot would meet the side of the ball.
Very high spin — the ball may knuckle unpredictably. Pull back slightly on the wrap to control the spin into the 300-500 rpm sweet spot.
The curve needs significant work. First master the contact point — inside of the foot on the side of the ball — then worry about adding pace.
Solid developing curve — your technique has the right shape. Keep building the spin rate and you will have a genuinely dangerous weapon.
High spin rate — the ball really bends. Watch that you do not over-curl it wide. Aim to bend it INTO the target, not past it.
Great blend of pace and curl. At this level, try disguising your run-up so defenders cannot predict which way the ball will bend.
Good curve with controlled pace. Next step: practice with a ball played to you on the move — make the curl work from a dynamic situation.
Too flat for a chip — you need to get under the ball more. Use a sharp stabbing motion and cut underneath the ball to generate steep lift.
Not enough lift. A chip needs 35-55 degrees. Get your foot under the ball with a short, decisive downward strike rather than a long scoop.
Chip is barely leaving the ground. Focus on striking the very bottom of the ball with a stiff ankle — the steep downward cut generates the height.
Too steep — the ball will land well short. Strike slightly less far under the ball to achieve a 40-55 degree angle, not 60+.
Way too high — almost straight up. You are digging under the ball too much. A chip should float, not rocket skyward. Shallower contact point.
Good instinct but too steep for the distance. For chips from further out, you want a shallower angle around 38-50 degrees so it carries to the target.
Far too much pace for a chip. Use a stabbing, cushioned touch with minimal backswing. Let the angle do the work, not the force.
Slightly too firm for a delicate chip. Reduce your backswing and focus on a short, sharp contact — minimal force with maximum angle.
Chip is too soft — it will barely clear the keeper. A chip needs to be decisive with a sharp stab. Add more intent into the contact.
Very little backspin — the ball will run on after landing. Strike with a sharper downward angle to generate backspin that checks the ball.
Good backspin level. The ball will check nicely on landing. This is the spin range you want for a chip that stops quickly after it lands.
Too much sidespin on the chip — it will drift offline. Keep your foot straighter underneath the ball to generate pure backspin.
You are scooping rather than chipping. A chip needs a sharp, stabbing contact under the ball — not a long sweeping motion through it.
Excellent chip — good height, right pace, controlled backspin. This ball would clear a keeper and drop sharply. Great technique.
Perfect chip. The backspin will bring it down quickly after it clears the keeper. Try this from further away and vary the landing spot.
Exceptional chip — steep, soft, and with good backspin. This would beat any keeper who is off their line. Now practice it under game pressure.
Textbook chip shot. Soft enough, high enough, backspin to hold it. Try chipping moving balls and in 1v1 situations next.
Solid chip — the fundamentals are right. Now work on distance control. Practice landing in a 3-foot circle at different ranges from goal.
Very good chip technique. For your next challenge, try chipping a ball that is rolling toward you rather than stationary.
Nice loft and controlled pace. Chips in this range will clear a rushing keeper. Work on reproducing this distance on every attempt.
Great height on that chip. The steeper the angle, the less forward carry — account for this when you aim so the ball drops into the right zone.
Beautiful floaty chip with controlled backspin. Focus on replicating this consistently under pressure — it needs to feel automatic in a 1v1.
Getting under the ball for a chip takes practice. Drill: place the ball and focus only on striking the very bottom 10mm of it. Nothing else.
Chip technique needs work. Key mechanics: stiff ankle, short stabbing motion under the ball. Watch chip shots in slow-motion to visualise it.
Elite chip for your age — perfect height, pace, and backspin. Try chipping from outside the box and aiming for the top corner.
Decent chip — slightly under-launched but will still clear most keepers off their line. Get to 40+ degrees consistently on your angle.
Good height and spin — the shape is right. Focus on landing accuracy: try to land every chip within a 2-yard target zone.
Chip technique struggling. Go back to basics: practice pushing the ball under a cone just in front of you — that is the feeling you are after.
Reasonable chip but a bit too much sidespin. Keep your foot straighter at contact to generate clean backspin for a controlled flight.
Weak foot needs regular dedicated work — it will not improve on its own. Give your non-dominant foot 15 minutes of focused practice every session.
Getting some pace on the weak foot — good start. Focus on the contact point first: laces through the ball, same technique as your strong foot.
Decent weak foot pace. Your plant foot positioning is key — plant it beside the ball pointing at your target for better direction control.
Good weak foot effort. Follow through fully after contact — do not pull your leg back. Let the foot swing all the way through the ball.
Strong weak foot kick for your age. This will make you much harder to defend. Keep training this side equally with your dominant foot.
Impressive weak foot — this is a real weapon. Defenders cannot afford to show you onto your weaker side anymore, which creates space.
Inconsistent foot angle on the weak foot — the ball is going unpredictable directions. Focus on your plant foot: it must point at the target.
Too much angle variance on the weak foot. Plant your non-kicking foot firmly beside the ball and keep your eyes down through contact.
Weak foot pace is still quite low. Each week try to add 2 mph to your weak foot strike. Consistent practice is the only solution here.
Closing the gap between feet. Keep at it — players who can strike equally with both feet are extremely difficult to defend against.
Very off-center weak foot contact. Slow the kick right down — strike a stationary ball slowly to find the correct contact point first.
Slightly off-center on the weak foot. This is normal early in development. Lock the ankle and aim to hit the exact center of the ball every time.
Really solid weak foot strike. Clean contact, decent pace, good angle. You are well on your way to being a genuinely two-footed player.
Excellent weak foot kick — better than most players your age. Can you add options: curve the ball with your weak foot too?
Weak foot contact is very rough. Fix: 50 weak-foot-only passes against a wall every day. Watch the improvement in just two weeks.
Good weak foot session. Two-footed players get far more opportunities in matches and are much harder to mark. This is a great investment.
That is a genuinely strong weak foot. You are ahead of where most players your age are with their non-dominant foot. Keep pushing this.
Weak foot is very early in development — that is completely fine. Kick a ball against a wall 20 times with your weak foot every single day.
High launch angle on weak foot — you are getting under the ball. Lean slightly forward over the ball to keep the trajectory flatter.
Decent weak foot but inconsistent. Set a goal: 10 weak foot strikes per practice. Repetition is the only way to build non-dominant foot muscle memory.
Consistent weak foot technique — this is great to see. You are building a real two-footed ability that will serve you throughout your career.
Weak foot coming along. To improve pace, exaggerate your follow-through — swing the leg fully past the ball after contact.
Strong weak foot strike — precise and controlled. Next challenge: weak foot only passing drills for your entire next training session.
Exceptional weak foot power and technique. This is a match weapon. Practice finishing with your weak foot from inside the penalty area.
Solid weak foot kick with controlled direction and respectable pace. Keep adding to both — you are building something genuinely useful.
Too soft for a penalty — a keeper can react and save this pace. Drive through with your laces and commit fully. Penalties demand decisiveness.
Decent penalty pace. Aim for the corners rather than down the middle — placement matters more than raw speed from 12 yards.
Good penalty pace and angle. At this speed and height the keeper has very little time to react. Pick your side early and commit to it.
Excellent penalty — power, placement, and a low angle. Your pre-kick routine appears solid. Keep replicating this every single time.
Off-center penalty contact — from 12 yards accuracy is everything. Practice aiming for cones in the corners on every penalty you take.
Good pace but off-center. Penalties are often lost in the run-up, not the strike. Slow the approach down and commit firmly to your target spot.
Too much height — this goes over the bar. Lean your body forward over the ball and drive through the center to keep it low.
Way too high — do not give the keeper this gift. Lower your body position and drive through the center of the ball with your body leaning over it.
Perfect penalty angle — low and powerful. The keeper must dive to ball level, making it very hard to save. Great body position and technique.
Solid penalty technique. Remember: pick your spot before stepping up, look at the ball — not the keeper — on your run-up, and trust the strike.
Poor contact on the penalty — scuffed or mis-struck. From 12 yards you must make clean contact. Practice full commitment on every strike.
Textbook penalty — low, powerful, accurate, minimal spin. You have the technique to be a reliable penalty taker in any situation.
Strong penalty. At this pace from 12 yards, the keeper needs to be in the air before you strike to have a chance. Good technique.
Too much spin on the penalty — the ball will curve away from your intended target. Strike straight through with your laces for accurate placement.
Almost along the ground — a well-positioned keeper will save this. Aim for ankle or knee height on the keeper: low but not ground-skimming.
That is a penalty that would score at any level. Perfect combination of power, placement, and low trajectory. You are a reliable penalty taker.
Penalties can be nerve-wracking to practice — keep at it. Focus on just three things: pick your spot, calm run-up, strike with your laces.
Good penalty foundation. Work on your run-up rhythm — a consistent approach makes it harder for keepers to read your intended direction.
Very good penalty. Pace and placement both solid. Practice from both sides of the area and with your weak foot to be a complete penalty taker.
Penalty has room to improve on both pace and accuracy. Focus on placement first — lock in the corner consistently, then add power once it is reliable.
Unstoppable penalty — keeper has no chance with this pace and placement combination. You have mastered the fundamentals of penalty technique.
Solid penalty kick. The next level is delaying your eye contact with the target as long as possible before striking to keep the keeper guessing.
Strong, controlled penalty. Minimal spin keeps the ball true to your target. Great technique — this is what penalty specialists train for hours.
Penalty needs more power and better angle control. Practice with a target — a cone in the bottom corner — to sharpen both at once.
Clinical penalty technique. Power, placement, and angle all dialed in. This is what separates penalty specialists — keep drilling this.
Free kick needs more pace to threaten the goal. Even a curling free kick needs enough speed to carry over the wall and still beat the keeper.
Good starting point. The spin is developing — work on combining the curl with enough pace to make it a genuine scoring threat.
Solid free kick — real curl and enough pace. Make sure you are clearing the wall. Practice with cones at the correct wall height and distance.
Excellent free kick technique. The spin will generate real bend in the flight. Time it to dip over the wall and away from the keeper's reach.
Outstanding free kick. Pace and high spin mean the ball will bend significantly and arrive with real pace — extremely dangerous to face.
Very little spin on the free kick — it will fly straight. Connect with the inside of your foot and follow through wide to generate curl.
Minimal curl. Wrap your instep around the side of the ball at contact and swing your leg across your body for more spin generation.
Extremely high spin — this will either curve too much or knuckle. Pull back slightly on the wrap to control the spin into the 300-500 rpm range.
Angle too flat — this will go into the wall. You need to lift the ball over the defensive wall. Strike lower on the ball to generate lift.
Too steep — free kick is clearing the bar. Get more forward with your body and strike through the mid-section of the ball.
Right angle to clear the wall and dip toward goal. At 22-40 degrees with good spin, the ball will rise over the wall then dip sharply. Keep this.
This free kick has a great dipping trajectory. High spin plus pace causes the ball to clear the wall then drop sharply — very hard to save.
Great technique. Now work on placement — practice bending it to the same corner consistently. Target practice is essential for set-piece specialists.
Solid technique for a mid-range free kick. For longer range, you need 5-10 mph more pace without losing spin — work on that combination.
Poor contact on the free kick. Take your time — set yourself properly: plant foot beside ball, pick your target, then commit to the contact.
That is a match-quality free kick. The bend, dip, and pace makes this a genuine scoring threat. Work on reproducing this every single time.
Strong free kick with well-controlled spin. Next step: practice from different angles, not just straight in front of goal.
Elite free kick for your age. The spin rate and pace combination is genuinely difficult to save. Practice this from both sides of center.
Free kicks take a lot of practice — keep going. Start by just practicing the contact point: inside of foot, side of ball. Add pace gradually.
Developing free kick — the curl is starting to appear. Push the follow-through right across your body after contact.
Consistent free kick with real curl. Start thinking about the target: top corner or bottom corner? Aim for a specific spot every time.
Nice technique. A 30-45 degree approach angle gives you more leverage on the inside-of-foot strike — try varying your run-up angle.
Very strong free kick. Develop a set routine — same steps, same run-up — so this becomes automatic and repeatable under match pressure.
Free kick went badly wrong — that is fine in practice. Reset, breathe, and focus only on the contact point for the next attempt.
Excellent first touch — very soft and controlled. The ball stays close to your feet, which is exactly what you want when receiving under pressure.
Great touch — soft and accurate. At this pace the ball stays in your personal space and you maintain full control. This is elite receiving.
Decent touch — slightly firm but manageable. Cushion the ball more by relaxing your foot at contact and letting it absorb the pace.
Touch is a bit heavy — the ball is getting away from you. Imagine your foot is a pillow: relax it completely at contact to absorb pace off the ball.
Touch is too firm — the ball is escaping. For a dribble touch, use a short, controlled contact with a completely relaxed foot.
Controlled touch with good contact duration. The longer, gentler contact means you have absorbed the pace well. Good technique for tight spaces.
Contact was slightly abrupt. Let your foot stay with the ball slightly longer to cushion it — a gentle following motion after contact.
Touch was slightly off-center — the ball may roll sideways. Use the inside of your foot for touches — it gives you the largest contact surface.
Off-center touch sent the ball sideways. Use the inside of your foot — not the toe or outside — for dribble touches. Biggest contact area wins.
Perfect dribble touch — soft, controlled, and on the ground. The ball stays at your feet. This under pressure is what separates good players.
Excellent first touch. Soft contact, ball under control, no bounce. Practice receiving from different angles and heights to be complete.
Your touch is sending the ball upward — too much foot angle at contact. Use the inside or top of your foot and angle it downward toward the ground.
Slight bounce on the touch — ball is rising. Guide the ball downward with your foot angle to keep it on the ground where you can play quickly.
Good outside-of-foot touch. This is a great skill for a touch-and-turn in one movement. Practice receiving and turning in a single fluid motion.
First touches take daily practice. Try receiving passes against a wall — kick it, let it come back, control it dead, repeat 50 times.
Heavy touch — the ball is escaping your control. Drill: juggle 10 times and then stop the ball dead on the ground. Repeat to feel soft contact.
Outstanding first touch — elite-level ball control. You can receive and immediately be in position to play. Keep this standard every session.
Brilliant touch. Soft, precise, and controlled. Next challenge: receive with your back to goal and touch the ball away from a defender in one move.
Consistent first touch developing. Keep working on receiving from different heights and angles to build a complete, reliable first touch.
Controlled and soft — the ball stays with you. Practice this at increasing pass speeds so your touch holds up under harder deliveries.
Technique is breaking down — this looks like fatigue. Take a 2-minute active rest: walk around, shake your legs out, then restart fresh.
Significant performance drop. Fatigue is badly affecting your technique. Quality over quantity — stop and rest rather than practice bad habits.
Curve ball suffering badly — this is fatigue. Rest at least 5 minutes before your next kick. Tired muscles cannot learn or retain technique.
Fatigue showing in your chip — inconsistent contact and poor angle. Stop, hydrate, and rest. Resume when you can reproduce your earlier form.
Weak foot breaking down under fatigue. Do not push through — weak foot technique needs full concentration, and fatigue destroys it.
Penalty technique collapsing — classic sign of fatigue. A tired penalty is a missed penalty. Rest fully before practicing penalties.
Free kick quality dropped sharply — rest now. Free kicks require precise technique that fatigue destroys completely. Come back tomorrow fresher.
Touch becoming heavy — a classic sign of fatigue. Your fine motor control is affected. End the session now. You have done enough good work today.
Speed and accuracy both declining across your session. Take 3 minutes off, drink water, and do 5 light jogs before your next kick.
High variance in your curl technique suggests fatigue is setting in. Reduce session volume — 10 quality kicks beats 30 tired ones.
